brief.head: Nobody’s watching
brief.text: The deepest anxiety is what others think, Amit Varma said, and it took him till middle age to see that no one is thinking of you. {011-C11}

brief.head: We are all stupid
brief.text: Each of us knows a handful of things well, Varma argued. In everything else we are stupid, so be humble, and don’t judge others. {011-C12}

brief.head: Your edge is you
brief.text: Chase trends or the algorithm and you lose your uniqueness, Varma said. “The only thing that separates me from the 8 billion people on this planet is me.” {011-C04}

brief.head: Shelling pine nuts
brief.text: Ghazala Wahab’s grandfather is not called loving: he shells pine nuts all day to reward the children. That, Varma said, is showing, not telling. {011-C08}

brief.head: Small tools, big jobs
brief.text: Unix is a way of thinking, not just a tool, Ajay Shah said: many small tools, strung together to perform any task. {011-C20}

thought.text: The problem with practical goals is that you’ll actually achieve them.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, arguing that purpose, not talent or targets, keeps people running

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on getting things done
lead.head: All the world’s a vegetable
body: Ajay Shah opened with a forecast for the merchandising trade: the slogan “just do it” was about to be overpowered by a new one, “Kaator re bhaaji”. Both hosts were wearing it on their t-shirts. {011-J01}
The words are Konkani. Over the next hour, Amit Varma unpacked them into rules for getting work done, and Shah steered the talk towards purpose.

The mantra comes from a story Jerry Pinto told Varma on *The Seen and the Unseen*. Abbé Faria, a Goan child prodigy born in 1756, was invited as a teenager to speak before the Queen of Portugal in Lisbon. On stage, facing the queen, the royalty and his own father, he froze.
His father leaned forward and hissed at him. In Varma’s rendering: “All these are vegetables. Cut the vegetables, cut the vegetables, cut the vegetables.” {011-C01}
Whatever we do in our lives, Varma said, “it boils down to cutting the vegetables, to building a habit, to routine”.
## Four slogans, two U-turns
Varma then offered four slogans, each pulling against the one before. The first was Nike’s: just do it. You get something right, he said, by getting it done again and again. {011-C02}

Shah tempered it. Repetition helps only if you can sense the gradient of the hill you are climbing. “It is possible to just keep doing the same thing over and over and being bad at it every single time,” he said.
Invited to contradict himself, Varma offered the second slogan: don’t do it, just be it. Decide who the best version of you is, he said, and let the habits flow from that self-image.
The third reversed the second: don’t be it, just do it. Praise children for their effort, not their intelligence. Verbs matter; adjectives don’t.

The fourth gathered up the rest: habits are everything. Ask a hundred writers about their goals and you cannot tell the good from the bad. Ask about their habits, Varma said, “and you will never be wrong”.
Shah’s method is to take on one habit at a time, for two or three months of focus, until it runs on autopilot. Six at once, he said, cannot be done.
## From tools to purpose
Varma demonstrated Roam Research, the note-taking tool he uses to prepare his episodes, and argued that the form of our input and output shapes how we think.
Shah’s choice was older. After 40 years around computers, he said, Unix and the command line remain the most productive and powerful environment there is. {011-R15}
Asked to zoom out, Shah set productivity aside for purpose. Practical goals are weak fuel, he argued, because once you reach them you are left asking what comes next.
Life organised around status markers, from the famous university to the top journal, is a poor operating system, he said, because it does not harness the mind. {011-C15}
The real superpowers, in his telling, are curiosity and endurance, put to work for a purpose.

Shah did not claim his technique was the right one. But each of us, he said, has to ask why we are here, and find “that marathon runner’s ability to run long, difficult journeys without the simple gratification of external validation”.

second.label: What talent is
second.head: Talent, rain or shine
second.deck: Amit Varma recalls a sportsman whose gift was getting up anyway
body: A top sportsperson, asked about his greatest talent, gave an answer Amit Varma read in the early 2000s and still talks about. It sounded very Dravid-esque, Varma said, but it was not Rahul Dravid, and he has failed to track it down. {#dravidesque}

The athlete ran every day at five. Suppose he woke with a cold, his goal for the year already met, a holiday coming and rain outside. He would still get up and run. That, he said, was talent. {011-S06}
We think of talent as natural genius, Varma said. Sometimes it is just the quality “which makes you dogged, which makes you go out there and do it and just get the job done”. {#dogged}

quote.text: I will still get up and go running in the rain. That’s talent.

second.caption: the athlete who ran in the rain

third.head: The pot thickens
body: A group of people was split into two halves, Amit Varma said. One half had a week to make a single pot, and could spend the week researching and planning it. The other was told to make as many pots as they wanted. {011-S02}
The planners read books and worked out in theory what makes a perfect pot. Varma pictured them taking online courses in “the art of clear pottery”, a nod to his own writing course. {011-J05}
The second group simply got the job done, again and again. The best pots came from them.
Ajay Shah added a caution. Iteration needs a sense of which way is uphill, he said; without one, people can stay bad forever. {011-C05}
third.caption: the pottery experiment

p2.title: Do it, be it, do it
p2.deck: Amit Varma’s four slogans for getting things done, and Ajay Shah’s case for purpose over productivity

sections.label: The first slogan
sections.head: Get it done, then get it right
sections.caption: getting it done before getting it right
body: Every venture, Amit Varma said, involves a trade-off between getting it done and getting it right. He has a bias towards getting it done. {011-C02}
For a writer, the first draft is where you get it done: “Take a dump of the brain.” Rodin, he said, did not fashion *The Thinker* out of thin air. He took a block of stone and edited it. {011-J11}
His friend Vinay Sitapati put it another way: “Never let perfection be the enemy of production.”

The YouTuber Ali Abdaal needed half a year of two videos a week to reach his 50th video and his first thousand subscribers. Everyone sucks at the start, Varma said, so anyone driven by validation stops before getting good. {011-C03}
## Standards and momentum

Ajay Shah agreed, then tempered it. Iteration needs a sense of the gradient of the hill you are climbing. India celebrates *jugaad*, he said, which to him is “just a fancy name given for people who do things really badly”. {011-C05}
His role in India, he said, has been to push standards: “No, this ain’t good enough. Can we try harder?” But nobody should be paralysed by perfectionism.

~ Varma’s own apprenticeship was his blog, India Uncut, from around 2003-04: five posts a day, about 8,000 in five years. “There was no anxiety about getting it perfect,” he said. “It was me thinking aloud.”

quote.text: You get something right by getting it done again and again and again.

sections.label: The second slogan
sections.head: A reader, not a timetable
sections.caption: being the best version of yourself
body: Told by Ajay Shah to contradict himself, Amit Varma obliged, “for we contain multitudes, as the great Walt Whitman once said”. {011-J09} His second slogan: don’t do it, just be it.

Most of us build a habit by timetable, he said: read every evening from seven to eight. Day one goes well, and day two. By day three you fall off the wagon, and by day four somebody is wrong on the internet and you have to correct them. {011-J06}
Then the damage spreads to your self-image. You decide you are not a reader, perhaps a Netflix kind of person, and the game is over.

Instead, picture the best version of yourself: a self-taught polymath who, when bored, picks up a book and not the phone. Own that identity, Varma said, and the habits flow from it. Miss a day and it means nothing. {011-C06}
## The image problem

Shah asked about the image we show the world: it can keep us accountable, or breed imposter syndrome. Varma’s answer was that it took him into middle age to realise that no one is thinking of you. No one, he said, is taking screenshots to shame you on Twitter, “or actually in my case, they are”. {011-J08}
~ Social media makes things worse, he argued, by setting our real selves against the projected selves of others.

quote.text: Where your self-image drives your habits and not the other way around.

sections.label: The third slogan
sections.head: Verbs matter, adjectives don’t
sections.caption: praising effort, not cleverness
body: The third slogan undid the second: don’t be it, just do it. Amit Varma took it from a study by Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck, which he found through an episode of the *Huberman Lab* podcast. {011-R07}

Children given a common task were split in two. One half was praised for attributes: you’re so intelligent. The other half was praised for effort. The first group did worse in later tests, and some might even cheat. The second kept doing well. {011-C07}

Varma looks back on his own life with “a touch of regret and sadness”. Things came easily to him: an exam others studied 20 hours for, he could do in 20 minutes. “And this is a great trap,” he said. {011-S07}
## A number on the forehead

Ajay Shah, by his own account the lucky child who blossomed at the right age, called India’s early labelling of children as smart or dumb “a truly toxic thing”. Everybody, he said, started painting a number on his forehead. {011-S08}
Age-sorted classrooms, he argued, are an industrial-revolution idea. People who work in education know that different people blossom differently, with no fixed age. {011-C13}
~ Talent, Shah said, is “one of the most harmful words”. The two superpowers are curiosity and endurance.

quote.text: Humans are unruly, unpredictable creatures and we all blossom in different dimensions at different rates.

sections.label: The fourth slogan
sections.head: Two hundred words a day
sections.caption: habits as compound interest
body: The last slogan gathered up the rest: habits are everything. Amit Varma borrowed a line from James Clear’s *Atomic Habits*: “Habits are the compound interest of self-improvement.” {#compound}

His thought experiment comes from his writing class. Gather a hundred writers, from great to bad, and ask about their goals: you cannot tell them apart. Ask about their processes and habits, and you will know who will make it. {011-C09}

Targets must survive a busy life. Writers who set themselves a thousand words a day, and then fail, slide into a *mujhse nahi hoga* spiral. Varma asks for 200, about what he speaks in a minute: his speaking speed, he said, is 160 to 170 words a minute. {#speed}
A gym membership builds no muscle, he added. Going to the gym does.
## One at a time

Ajay Shah linked it to the glucose monitor the hosts had discussed. Watching every meal is a heavy cognitive burden, he said, but a habit takes about two or three months of focus, after which it runs on autopilot. {011-C10}
Asked which habit he was glad he had built, Shah said he had organised his whole life around one purpose: more hours each day to read. {011-S09}
~ He keeps pushing away mundane things and decisions, he said, to reduce the burden of everyday life.

quote.text: You have to fight one thing at a time and it is solvable.

sections.label: The toolkit
sections.head: A second brain, with links
sections.caption: Roam Research and the second brain
body: Ajay Shah asked whether the world of productivity tools matters at all. He dislikes the word itself: “It’s too much of a managerial thing. It’s too much Taylorism for me.” {011-J15}
Amit Varma answered with a demonstration of Roam Research, the note-taking tool he uses to prepare his episodes. Its nested entries replaced the 40-page Word files he once scrolled through madly.

His notes on Ghazala Wahab’s *Born a Muslim* follow the book chapter by chapter. Shah’s notes for their Ukraine episode had detailed chapters, links and, “like a good academic”, a list of sources. That, Varma said, came from a lifetime’s habit of reading. {011-S10}
## The shape of thought
The form of our input and output matters, Varma argued. A day with a physical book sets one rhythm of mind; a day of scrolling and swiping sets a choppier one. {011-C17}
His friend Gautam John once looked at his smartphone, for anything other than calls, only between five and six in the evening. {011-S11}
The brain, Varma said, is a messy, impressionistic machine, which is why he likes Tiago Forte’s idea of a second brain. {011-C18}
~ Shah put in a word for two alternatives. Obsidian, which Varma noted is free, keeps notes as plain Markdown files; Org Mode in Emacs is very powerful, though it lacks a networked, shared version.

quote.text: All day we are taking in learnings that we do not retain.

sections.label: Ajay zooms out
sections.head: Credentials don’t run a life
sections.caption: purpose, curiosity and endurance
body: Amit Varma asked Ajay Shah to zoom out from tactics and say how he thinks one should live.

Many of us start out chasing simple things: an exam, a job, some money, or “the Louis Vuitton bag of the credentials”, the famous university, the famous journal, the festival book talk. That, Shah said, is a poor operating system, because it does not harness the mind. {011-C15}
He recalled a talk at which Rahul Dravid said he never thought about Sachin Tendulkar, and only tried to be the best Rahul Dravid he could be. {011-S12}
## Thirty years, one year
In research, Shah said, “journal orientation” is toxic advice because it switches off curiosity.

Years alone do not build experience, he argued. Write an eleventh paper like the first ten and no new ground is broken. What makes a year count is curiosity, endurance and a willingness to challenge the status quo. {011-C16}
His own journey, he said, has been the falling away of distractions, so that he stays connected to the core. In some weird way, he has been the same since he was a teenager.
~ Ever since the Greeks, Shah said, we have known that meaning comes from being part of something bigger than oneself. Simple objectives harness only ten per cent of each of us. {#tenpercent}

quote.text: It’s a poor operating system, most importantly, because it actually does not harness the mind.

side.boxText: Abbé Faria, born José Custódio de Faria in Candolim in 1756, left India after a rebellion, took part in the French Revolution and became one of the fathers of hypnotism. Alexandre Dumas named a character in *The Count of Monte Cristo* after him. {011-R22}

contQuote.text: You could be doing thirty years of the same thing over and over, and you’ve actually not been on a life journey of growing and becoming a bigger and better and more interesting person.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A prodigy, a delay, a prize and a finished program

stories.start: And he told me this brilliant story about a gentleman named Abe Faria
stories.end: So a a remarkable man born in nearby Candleim, who achieved so much.
stories.caption: the whisper in Lisbon
stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells Jerry Pinto’s story of a Goan prodigy
stories.head: The boy who froze before a queen
body: José Custódio de Faria was born in 1756 in Candolim, when Goa was a Portuguese colony. His father was a priest and his mother a nun. They joined the church after having him, Amit Varma explained, and separated.
Ajay Shah placed it before the Battle of Plassey. “There you go,” said Varma. {011-J04}

His father treated him as a prodigy and took him around to be educated. By his teens the boy was famous for his brilliant sermons, and the Queen of Portugal invited him to speak in Lisbon, then, Shah noted, one of the great cities of the world.
Varma set the scene with relish: the queen in her green silk emerald dress, and all the royalty of Lisbon “in their breeches and their gowns, with magnificent smiles and frowns”. {011-J03}
On the stage, with everyone who mattered to him staring out of the darkness, the boy froze. No words came.
His father leaned forward and hissed in Konkani: *kaator re bhaaji*. All these are vegetables, Varma translated. Cut the vegetables. {011-C01}

Faria’s adventures did not end there. Caught up in a rebellion, he had to leave India. He took part in the French Revolution and was imprisoned, alone, on an island. There he remembered his father’s words, built a mental framework and became one of the fathers of hypnotism.
~ In *The Count of Monte Cristo*, Varma added, Alexandre Dumas named a character after him.
stories.why: Big, frightening moments shrink when you treat them as a pile of vegetables to chop. Whatever we do in our lives, Varma said, comes down to cutting the vegetables: to habit and routine. {011-S01}
stories.postscript: The hosts wore the mantra on t-shirts made by Varma’s friend Narendra Shenoy. {011-J01}

stories.start: And in this, I want to talk about a story of you and me.
stories.end: we should have started when we conceived of it, not waited for too long
stories.caption: the year before Episode One
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah and Amit Varma disagree about their own show
stories.head: Sharpening an axe, or not
body: By August 2022, in Udaipur, Ajay Shah and Amit Varma were sure they would make this show, and were debating names for it. The first episode arrived more than a year later.
Shah put the delay down to ambition. They had “dreams of quality and perfectionism”, he said, and a messy, jugaad-style start did not meet the bar. {011-S04}

Varma pushed back. Abraham Lincoln, he said, would spend five of six hours sharpening the axe before chopping a tree. {#lincoln} But the hosts had not been sharpening anything. Varma had simply been procrastinating.
~ What finally got it moving was a chance brainstorm with a producer friend, Vartika: she was a professional, they could get her to do it, and once it had momentum they could figure out the rest.
stories.why: It is easy to pass off procrastination as preparation. You need standards and momentum both, and the hosts disagree on the balance: Varma still says they should have started when they conceived the show. {#started}

stories.start: A question that I sometimes ask people in our circles
stories.end: where you've defined purpose differently, and I find that really interesting
stories.caption: the Nobel Prize question
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the Nobel question he asks friends
stories.head: Not playing the Nobel game
body: Amit Varma sometimes asks people in his circles a question: of all the guests on *The Seen and the Unseen*, who is most likely to win a Nobel Prize? The standard answer is the economist Karthik Muralidharan, who, Varma said, is clearly on that track.
Varma’s own rule is to name the most brilliant person he knows. On his show, at the risk of embarrassing him, that was Ajay Shah. When Varma told him so, Shah said he was not on that track. {#track}
With great sadness, Varma agreed. Shah, he said, had defined his purpose differently and was playing a different kind of game. {011-S13}
~ People who do play that game, like Muralidharan, are doing amazing work, Varma said, and more power to them.
stories.why: Prizes reward those who play a particular game. Someone who has defined his purpose differently, Varma suggested, can be brilliant and still choose not to play it. Shah, by his own account, is not on that track.

stories.start: So as an example, hiding inside that is a typesetting system called tech
stories.end: the people just put it on a frame and put it on their walls
stories.caption: Donald Knuth’s TeX
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s tribute to a program that is finished
stories.head: A Taj Mahal made of code
body: Hidden inside the Unix toolchain, Ajay Shah said, is TeX, a professional typesetting system used by many publishers. Many of the great books of the world are set with it. {011-R16}

Its main author, Donald Knuth, is one of the world’s great thinkers and spent his whole life polishing it. Now that he is old, he says TeX is finished: it needs no further feature, and it has no recorded bugs. {#finished}
The code is open, and anyone may build on it. Knuth asks only that after he is gone, they call it something else. “This is my Taj Mahal,” he says. “I built this.” {011-S14}
~ When a bug does turn up, Knuth writes the finder a cheque. The finders frame it and hang it on their walls.
stories.why: TeX shows that a program can actually be finished, and gives, Shah said, a flavour of the maturity of Unix. Most software, by contrast, is “just some rubbish layered on rubbish”. {011-C19}

quiz.q: What did Abbé Faria’s father hiss at him in Lisbon, and what does it mean?
quiz.a: “Kaator re bhaaji”: Konkani for “all these are vegetables, cut the vegetables”.

quiz.q: In the pottery experiment Amit Varma described, which group made the best pots?
quiz.a: The group told to make as many pots as they liked.

quiz.q: What did Ali Abdaal advise new YouTubers to do before looking at their metrics?
quiz.a: Make two videos a week for two years: about 200 videos.

quiz.q: What did the study by Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck find about praising children?
quiz.a: Children praised for intelligence did worse; those praised for effort kept improving.

quiz.q: Which Indian cricketer said he only tried to be the best version of himself?
quiz.a: Rahul Dravid, who said he never thought about Sachin Tendulkar.

quiz.q: Around what single purpose has Ajay Shah organised his whole life?
quiz.a: Getting more hours each day to read, by cutting mundane tasks.
